issues.legal_issue: A special summary procedure for evicting unauthorised occupants of public property does not violate equality merely because an ordinary civil remedy may also be available or because the procedure applies to a distinct class of property.
material_facts: The challenged procedure applied to unauthorised occupants of premises belonging to a municipal corporation.
The law provided a special procedure for eviction, while eviction could also be pursued through an ordinary suit in some cases.
The special procedure was intended to provide a speedy method of recovering public property.
issues.conclusion: The special procedure did not violate Article 14 on the ground that the Commissioner had an unguided choice between that procedure and an ordinary suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14, legislation may establish a special procedure for a distinct class of cases when its purpose and policy provide guidance for applying that procedure. Applying Maganlal Chhagganlal Private Limited v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, the Court held that a special speedy procedure for recovering public property is not invalid merely because another procedure may be available; Northern India Caterers Private Ltd. v. State of Punjab no longer governed the issue.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_summary_evic: A person challenged the constitutionality of a summary procedure used to recover property.
predicates.unauthorised_occupation_of_public_proper: The proceeding concerned a person's unauthorised occupation of property belonging to a public body.
predicates.legislature_provided_special_speedy_proc: The legislature established a special process intended to recover the public body's property speedily.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a special speedy process for recovering public property from an unauthorised occupant, the process is not invalid merely because another remedy may be available.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative officer's authority to decide whether a person should be evicted from public property is not unreasonable merely because the officer acts for the public body that owns the property.
material_facts: The Commissioner, or a delegated Deputy Commissioner, was authorised to determine whether the statutory grounds for eviction existed.
The premises belonged to the Corporation, whose highest officer was the Commissioner.
The Court found no personal interest of the Corporation in the eviction and treated the Corporation as representing public interest.
An appeal was available against the Commissioner's decision.
issues.conclusion: The Commissioner's role in deciding whether to commence eviction did not make the procedure unreasonable on the ground that he was judge in his own cause.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that an administrative officer's performance of a public duty to protect public interest is not disqualified merely because the public body owns the property. A wrong exercise of power may be corrected on appeal; the procedure was not invalid under Article 19(1)(f) on this ground.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_eviction_pro: A person challenged the constitutionality of a procedure for eviction from property.
predicates.public_official_decides_eviction_eligibi: A public official decides whether the grounds for eviction are established.
predicates.official_acts_for_public_interest: The official acts in a public duty on behalf of a public body and has no personal interest in the eviction.
predicates.decision_is_appealable: The official's decision may be challenged through an appeal.

issues.definition: When an appealable eviction decision is made by a public official acting in a public duty without a personal interest, the official's role alone does not make the procedure unreasonable.

issues.legal_issue: A procedure for eviction is not an unreasonable restriction merely because the decision-maker cannot compel witnesses or an appeal lies to the government rather than an ordinary court, if the affected person can present an explanation and evidence and courts remain open to address injustice or denial of natural justice.
material_facts: Before an eviction order, the affected person was entitled to notice of the grounds and a reasonable opportunity to give an explanation and produce evidence.
The Commissioner had no special statutory power to compel witnesses to attend.
An appeal lay to the State Government rather than an ordinary court.
Courts remained open to address abuse of justice, miscarriage of justice, or violation of natural justice.
issues.conclusion: The procedure did not impose an unreasonable restriction on the right protected by Article 19(1)(f) because the affected person could present evidence, the State Government could hear the appeal, and judicial redress remained available for specified injustices.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a reasonable opportunity to explain and produce evidence suffices even without a special power to summon witnesses. An appeal to the State Government rather than a court is not inherently unreasonable, and judicial review remains available for abuse of justice, miscarriage of justice, or breach of natural justice.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_eviction_pro: A person challenged the constitutionality of a procedure for eviction from property.
predicates.affected_person_can_explain_and_produce_: The person facing eviction receives an opportunity to explain the case and produce evidence.
predicates.appeal_heard_by_government: An appeal from the eviction decision is heard by a government body rather than an ordinary court.
predicates.decision_may_be_reviewed_for_injustice: Courts remain available to address injustice or a violation of natural justice in the decision-making process.

issues.definition: Where an affected person can explain and produce evidence, the absence of witness-compulsion powers and an appeal to government rather than an ordinary court do not make the procedure unreasonable if the decision can be challenged for injustice.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to serve an eviction order that contains reasons does not, on the facts of this case, invalidate the order, although authorities should serve reasoned orders.
material_facts: The orders were not served on the affected persons.
The Court characterised the failure to serve them as inefficiency but found no infirmity in the orders.
issues.conclusion: The failure to serve the reasoned orders did not invalidate them, but the authorities should serve orders that state the reasons for their decision.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found no infirmity in the orders because reasons had been given, while stating that authorities should serve orders containing those reasons.

predicates.eviction_order_contains_reasons: The authority records reasons for making an eviction order.
predicates.reasons_not_served_on_affected_person: The authority does not serve the reasoned order on the person affected.

issues.definition: If an eviction order contains reasons but those reasons are not served on the affected person, the order is not invalidated on that basis, but the reasoned order should be served.
